title: When AI Labs Rival Nations
dek: A Long Read Sunday tour through the week's biggest ideas: the Misanthropic Statement unites safetyists and accelerationists against Anthropic on the eve of its IPO, raising a bigger question about whether AI labs now rival states. Plus handoverism, why every startup is converging on AI transformation, and the bitter lesson coming for how we organize work.

oneIdea.headline: The most powerful company is starting to compete with the most powerful institutions.
oneIdea.summary: Across history, church, state, and private enterprise have constantly jostled for relative power. Social networks already strained that balance with unprecedented breadth, depth, and fortunes. AI takes it to a new level because it isn't just competing for our time. It's competing to change how we do everything. When even friendly observers say Anthropic is on track to be the most powerful company on Earth and needs sovereign-level transparency, the question shifts to whether private enterprise past a certain scale needs democratic norms. Running alongside that: whether humanity should ever hand control to AI, and how much of our own process we should hand to agents.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Dependence on a supplier too large to challenge
items.body: Some who agreed with the statement against Anthropic would not sign for fear of losing access to its models. The NHS knows this position: two clinical system suppliers hold most of general practice, and complaints are muted accordingly. NLW worries about a company too powerful to cross; Zitron would say the power is financial and may not last. Either way, the remedy for a buyer is the same: more than one supplier, and data we can move.

items.title: Handing over decisions
items.body: The handover argument sounds abstract, but a small version is already in clinic. Each time a triage tool sets urgency, or a scribe drafts the plan, a decision has been part-delegated. The professional position is clear and worth restating: the tool may propose, the registered clinician decides and is accountable. Suppliers should say plainly which steps their product takes without a human.

items.title: Agents and the practice rota
items.body: The advice to stop designing agents around job titles is aimed at software firms and has little direct relevance yet. The useful part is unlearning: when automating a task such as recall letters or document filing, ask what outcome is needed, not how the last person did it. Audit the result, since nobody will have designed the steps.

the_other_side.text: Zitron, in a paid piece of which only the opening is free to read, would not accept that an AI lab rivals a state. His argument is that the capabilities and returns of AI have been overstated, and that the labs' standing was manufactured: had the press not flattered OpenAI and Anthropic early on, he says, they could not have raised the money. He treats talk that AI is "going to literally destroy everything tomorrow" as another form of promotion. The free section does not discuss the statement against Anthropic or the idea of handing control to AI.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is where the labs' power comes from: what the technology can do, or the capital and attention committed to it. Both accept as fact that Anthropic is now among the most valuable companies in the world, that critics from opposite camps signed a statement against it, and that money on this scale buys political weight. The empirical question is whether that power survives a funding downturn; the observable is whether Anthropic can meet its compute commitments from revenue, as its first public accounts will show. The residue is worldview: whether to fear a company for being too capable or to distrust it for claiming to be. For Whittemore to be vindicated, the lab's influence over law and markets must keep growing with its revenues. For Zitron, it must shrink once investors stop funding the losses. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both think the labs face too little outside scrutiny. Watch the first public accounts.

headlines.headline: The Misanthropic Statement lands on the eve of Anthropic's IPO
headlines.summary: Organized by the Center for AI Safety, the statement accuses Anthropic of racing to build recursively self-improving AI while using safety branding to court investors, employees, and the public. It also says the company has quietly weakened its safety pledges and lobbied for self-serving regulation. It arrives as the IPO and Nvidia's defanging push Anthropic's relative power to an all-time high.

headlines.headline: Anthropic is not a safe AI company, and we must reject its reckless attempt to amass power in the name of the greater good.
headlines.summary: The signers are open-letter regulars from the safety community, plus strange bedfellows like arch-accelerationist Beff Jezos. Steven Pinker is listed first.

headlines.headline: Safetyists and accelerationists signed for opposite reasons
headlines.summary: Safetyists worry that Anthropic's alleged safety theater undermines real safety legislation. Accelerationists appear to have signed on to the line about Anthropic amassing power, the same concern they've raised against its advocacy around Chinese open source.

headlines.headline: Anthropic is currently on track to be the most powerful company on Earth.
headlines.attribution: Thomas Wolf, co-founder of Hugging Face, explaining his signature
headlines.summary: Wolf said he has friends at Anthropic and wouldn't have used the word 'reckless.' He signed anyway because that level of impact demands transparency and openness close to, or even higher than, that of a sovereign government, and he doesn't think Anthropic is on track to deliver it.

headlines.headline: Some who agreed were afraid to sign
headlines.summary: Wolf says entrepreneurs, executives, and researchers shared the concerns but feared consequences for their careers or their access to models. Whether or not the fear is justified, he calls it a worrying early signal of concentrated power in itself.

headlines.headline: The real tension is an institutional balance of powers
headlines.summary: NLW argues that a central tension of this moment is the ebb and flow of power among societal institutions. From the Renaissance onward, church, state, and private enterprise have constantly traded relative position.

headlines.headline: Even the Medici had to go through the church
headlines.summary: Early transnational business actors like the Medici still worked through state and religious power to rise. We remember Cosimo and Lorenzo, but the family likely saw its true apotheosis generations later, when a Medici became pope. Later, the East India Company blurred the line between private and state power.

headlines.headline: Social networks broke the old breadth and depth limits
headlines.summary: Facebook famously surged past every major organized religion in membership. Unlike food companies competing for a few meal slots, social media competes for every waking hour. As Reed Hastings put it, Netflix's main competitor on the margin is sleep.

headlines.headline: Tech fortunes created a new class of actor
headlines.summary: The combined breadth and depth of tech companies produced fortunes beyond any historical comparison. That made a new category of actor: leaders who operate almost as transnational entities on their own, with governments still jostling over whether and how to rebalance.

headlines.headline: AI isn't competing for our time. It's competing to change how we do everything
headlines.summary: Social networks wanted our attention. AI's implication is changing how individuals and organizations do everything. NLW argues that the speed and scale of that growth create a new societal challenge about institutional power, separate from any specific questions of AI risk.

headlines.headline: The most powerful company is now competing to be the most powerful institution
headlines.summary: Anthropic doesn't have tanks and planes, so it's a bit over the top, but NLW says it's a lot less crazy than it sounds. The question he's tracking: do we need democratic norms for private enterprise once it reaches a certain scale?

headlines.headline: Handoverism will make strange alliances too
headlines.summary: One of Max Tegmark's five reasons for signing was that Anthropic leans hardest into building conscious beings with rights rather than controllable tools. NLW sets that characterization aside but says this is where he aligns most with safety advocates, despite very different views on other risks.

headlines.headline: Handoverism: humanity survives but hands its future to AI
headlines.summary: A widely shared essay this week defined handoverism as humanity entrusting the direction of its future entirely to AI. It cited Scott Alexander: if a godlike AI were verified as aligned, why not prompt it to 'please arrange the world as you see fit?'

headlines.headline: The handoff language comes from Anthropic's own founders
headlines.summary: Bill Gurley amplified the debate by citing co-founder Tom Brown: 'There is going to be a handoff where humanity will hand off control to transformative AI.' He also cited Dario Amodei's 'Machines of Loving Grace,' which imagines an AI-run economy distributing resources to humans. Gurley's question: are you prepared to receive your resources based on criteria an AI determines?

headlines.headline: If that belief informs Anthropic's corporate objectives, it belongs in the risk factor sections of its S-1. It isn't there today.
headlines.summary: Gurley, who calls himself decidedly anti-handoverism, also argues that anyone drafting, advocating for, or enacting AI regulation should have to disclose where they stand on the question.

headlines.headline: Expect the handoverism debate to get much bigger
headlines.summary: OpenAI is clearly carving out the opposite position, that humans should stay in control. NLW argues that gives it every incentive to keep this conversation on the agenda.

headlines.headline: Every AI startup is converging on AI transformation
headlines.summary: An investor essay, 'There Is Only One Company to Build,' argues that data, post-training, and inference companies are all climbing the value chain toward selling enterprise AI transformation. Even Cognition leans on its deployment motion. Everything below that layer (data, models, inference) is commoditizing; delivering a business outcome isn't.

headlines.headline: The training-data business is an on-ramp to the enterprise
headlines.summary: The playbook: run a data business for the labs, as Mercor, Scale, and Handshake have, to generate cash and gain proximity and credibility. Then pivot to enterprise AI. 'We do a lot of business with the labs' is a good way to earn credibility with, say, Bank of America.

headlines.headline: Enterprises don't want software. They want salvation through AI
headlines.summary: The essay's punchline: nobody wants to buy software, because buying software sucks. Companies want to buy a change in their business, and you can charge more for selling the change. There are really only two companies to build: you build intelligence or you diffuse it.

headlines.headline: Is 'diffusion software' a phase or the new normal?
headlines.summary: NLW flags the usual exaggeration in 'there is only one thing' framings, but says converging features across software companies give the idea merit. His open question: is this true only for the next five to ten years while intelligence diffuses, or for software from here on out?

headlines.headline: The bitter lesson is coming for software engineering
headlines.summary: Legora's CTO argues that prescribing interfaces, abstractions, and architecture to coding agents is a temporary division of labor. Our belief in superior human judgment on systems design is about to get Rich Sutton's bitter lesson: general systems left to find their own methods beat ones packed with human constraints.

headlines.headline: Stop building agents to mirror the org chart
headlines.summary: The agent-as-teammate model gives each agent standing responsibilities, memory, and a role mapped to a human job. In practice, NLW says, power users set objectives and guardrails and let a coordinator agent spin up whatever sub-agents it needs. He calls it the bitter lesson for digital organizational management.

headlines.headline: No process baggage can be an advantage
headlines.summary: NLW built How We Got Here's video pipeline in Claude Code without being a video editor. With no existing workflow to adapt to, the models designed their own approach. He admits the output is under-maximized, but he went from zero to animated videos in the show's first week.

headlines.headline: Our job now is unlearning
headlines.summary: Experts who unlearn their old methods and give agents the leash to build agent-native processes have a real edge. NLW's broader point is that everyone has a non-trivial task: dropping assumptions about the right way to organize agents' work instead of forcing it to mirror our own.
